newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Refugees say many dead in east Zaire's Uvira.
newsitem.headline: Refugees say many dead in east Zaire's Uvira.

text.p: Burundian refugees fleeing fighting in Zaire said on Tuesday that Tutsi rebels controlled the eastern town of Uvira after battles with Zairean troops in which hundreds of people were killed.

"At Uvira the situation is bad. There is nobody there except the Banyamulenge military and the bodies of people killed in the fighting. I saw hundreds of corpses in the streets," said Malaishi Bilemo, who left Uvira on Monday.
Refugees said Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels took Uvira, at the northern end of Lake Tanganyika, on Friday. The town, they said, was thoroughly looted and lacking food, medicines and water.
Up to 1,500 Burundian Hutus have arrived at Gatumba close to the Zaire border. They say the Banyamulenge rebels told them to go home to Burundi.
The refugees, who started to arrive in Burundi on Monday, are the first eyewitnesses to come out of Uvira, which was home to 100,000 people.
Ethnic Tutsi Banyamulenge rebels say they are resisting a campaign of persecution by authorities in Zaire's South Kivu region.

"In Zaire everything has changed. The Zairean military who were there have fled and it is now a group of Banyamulenge from the hills in charge. The new people are good. They did not kill us but they told us to go back home," said refugee Andre Misagwa.

The U.N. has revised downward an earlier estimate that 230,000 Burundian and Rwandan Hutu refugees fled camps north of Uvira because of fighting over the town. They now say 80,000 refugees fled leaving around 140,000 in place in the camps.

But with so few aid workers on the ground, the numbers remain unclear and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said up to 140,000 Burundian Hutu refugees could eventually return home.

UNHCR has long pushed for the repatriation of Burundian and Rwandan refugees from eastern Zaire camps and analysts say unilateral action by ethnic Tutsis advancing north towards the regional capital of Bukavu could help secure this objective.

Around 150,000 people have died in three years of fighting in Burundi since October 1993 when the country's first democratically elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted coup. Regional states imposed sanctions after Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army took power in a military coup on July 25.
Burundi's army has deployed hundreds of extra troops along its western frontier to prevent Hutu rebels from entering the country along with a possible refugee influx, according to a senior diplomat.
